warmup.q: FLP proves that no deterministic consensus algorithm can guarantee to terminate in an asynchronous network if one node may crash. Your Kubernetes cluster's etcd runs Raft. What does FLP mean for it?
options: etcd may occasionally decide two different values
etcd can't work at all, and only appears to by luck
etcd may stall while the network misbehaves, but never decides two different values
etcd escapes FLP by relying on synchronized clocks for safety
warmup.why: FLP is about termination, not safety. Raft keeps its safety properties under any timing and uses timeouts only to make progress, which works whenever the network delivers messages within roughly the timeout. When it doesn't, elections can repeat and writes stall, and nothing wrong is ever decided. Raft's safety doesn't depend on clocks at all; only leases for fast reads do, and etcd's default linearizable read avoids them.

sections.h: Total order broadcast: same messages, same order, every replica
sections.html:
The last lesson ended on something quorums can't do: a compare-and-set that two writers can't both win. This lesson finds the tool that can, and it starts from a different problem.

You run a payment ledger as a state machine: a piece of deterministic code that takes commands one at a time (authorize, capture, refund) and updates its state. Run three copies of it on three machines. If every copy starts from the same state and applies the same commands in the same order, every copy ends in the same state, with no further coordination. This is state machine replication, and it reduces "keep three ledgers identical" to "deliver the same commands in the same order to three places".

That delivery problem has a name: total order broadcast, also called atomic broadcast. It promises two things. Reliable delivery: if one replica delivers a message, every replica that doesn't crash delivers it. Total order: every replica delivers messages in the same order. Seen from a replica, total order broadcast is an append-only log that it reads from the start.

The simplest way to build one: send every message to one node, the sequencer, which numbers it 1, 2, 3 and forwards it to every replica. Messages can overtake each other on the way, so each replica holds back message 8 until it has delivered 7. A Kafka partition is this shape: the partition leader decides the order, and consumers read it by offset.

Now build the thing quorums couldn't. A compare-and-set register on top of the log: a client appends "if the value is null, set it to c2" as a command, and waits until its own replica applies that command. Every replica applies the same commands in the same order with the same code, so every replica computes the same answer for every CAS. The first CAS in the log wins and every later one fails, everywhere. Reads must go through the log too. A read answered straight from a replica's current state can lag behind a CAS that already returned to its client, and that is a stale read.

Where does it break? At the sequencer. If it crashes, nothing is ever delivered again. Promote a new one by hand, and you get minutes of downtime. Promote one automatically when the old one seems dead, and an old sequencer that was only slow may keep numbering messages too, so two replicas see two different message 8s: the split brain from the Replication track's first lesson. To replace the sequencer safely, the nodes must agree which message is number 8, despite crashes and delays. That is consensus.

try.title: Race six clients for one seat
steps: Run LogDemo. Six booking services send cas(null -> their name) for seat 12A through a total order broadcast with three replicas; messages take 1 to 20 ms and overtake each other.
Predict: can two clients both be told they got the seat? Will the replicas agree on who has it?
Run it again with -Pargs=7 for another seed. Then read the last two lines: 200 runs of mixed CAS and reads, with reads through the log, then reads that skip it.

seed 3: six clients race for seat 12A

c2's command reached the sequencer first, so it is first in every replica's log and wins everywhere. c5 heard "seat taken" before c2 heard "got the seat": answers travel separately, and order lives in the log, not in the replies. Reads that skip the log returned a stale value in 2 of 200 histories, which is rare enough to pass every test you would write by hand.

sections.h: Consensus is one problem in many disguises
sections.html:
Consensus is the problem of getting several nodes to decide one value. Each node may propose a value; all of them must end up deciding the same one. Four properties pin it down:

  • Uniform agreement: no two nodes decide differently.
  • Integrity: no node decides twice.
  • Validity: the decided value was proposed by someone.
  • Termination: every node that doesn't crash eventually decides.

The first three are safety properties, things that must never go wrong. Termination is a liveness property. Without it the problem is easy: name one node the dictator and let it decide. With it, the dictator's crash leaves everyone waiting forever, which is two-phase commit's coordinator problem.

Here is the lesson's main claim: consensus, a linearizable compare-and-set register, total order broadcast and fault-tolerant atomic commit are the same problem. Each can be built from any other, so a system that solves one has solved them all. The figure shows the reductions.

CAS to consensus: start a register at null; every proposer does compareAndExchange(null, myValue). Exactly one succeeds; every proposer decides the winner's value (the value it found, or its own if it found null). That is the lab's last exercise, three lines.

Consensus to log: run one consensus instance per log position. Instance 1 decides message 1, instance 2 decides message 2, and so on. Log to consensus: everyone appends their proposal; the first entry in the log is the decision. Log to CAS: section 1.

Atomic commit: the Transactions track's lesson on two-phase commit showed why 2PC alone isn't fault tolerant. Every participant votes, and the coordinator alone writes the decision; when it dies, prepared participants wait in doubt with their locks held. Make the decision itself a consensus value, chosen by a group of nodes, and any member of the group can finish the job. Gray and Lamport's Paxos Commit does this, and Spanner runs two-phase commit between groups that are each replicated with Paxos. The voting rule stays: commit only if every participant voted yes.

Not every atomic instruction is this strong. Maurice Herlihy showed in 1991 that each shared object has a consensus number: the most processes it can solve consensus for. A fetch-and-add counter can decide between two processes: each first writes its proposal where the other can read it, then increments the counter, and whoever got 0 wins; the one that got 1 knows exactly who beat it. With three, a process that got 2 can't tell which of the other two got 0. Compare-and-set works for any number. That is why lock-free algorithms on the JVM are built from compareAndSet, and why a coordination service exposes CAS, not just counters.

try.title: Build a log from compare-and-set, on paper
steps: You have an unlimited supply of linearizable registers slot[1], slot[2]... each with compareAndExchange(expected, new), which returns the value before. Write a few lines of Kotlin for append(msg) that puts msg in the first free slot, even with other clients appending at the same time.
Then say what a replica does to deliver the log in order, and why two replicas can never deliver different messages in slot 5.
try.expect:
fun append(msg: String): Int {
    var i = 1
    while (true) {
        val before = slot[i].compareAndExchange(null, msg)
        if (before == null) return i     // the slot was free: msg is entry i
        i++                              // someone else won slot i; try the next one
    }
}

A replica delivers by reading slot[1], slot[2]... in order and waiting while the next slot is still null. Each slot holds the value of the one CAS that won it, and a linearizable register shows that one value to everybody, so slot 5 can't hold different messages for different replicas. You have built total order broadcast from CAS. If a client crashes between winning a slot and telling anyone, the message is still in the log; a client that wants exactly-once must check whether its message is already there before retrying.

sections.h: FLP: no algorithm can promise to finish, and how real ones get around it
sections.html:
In 1985 Fischer, Lynch and Paterson proved a result now known as FLP: in an asynchronous system, no deterministic consensus algorithm can guarantee termination if even one node may crash. Every algorithm that never decides wrongly has some schedule of message delays in which it never decides at all.

The model matters. Asynchronous means no bounds on message delay or on how slowly a node runs, and no clocks to measure them. The intuition is the one from the Faults, time and truth track: without timing, a crashed node and a slow one look identical. An algorithm that waits for a node may wait forever. An algorithm that moves on without it may move on while the slow node's vote was the deciding one. The proof shows an adversary that controls delivery order can keep the algorithm on the fence indefinitely.

FLP doesn't say consensus is impossible in practice, and it doesn't say safety must break. It says termination can't be guaranteed in that model. Real systems step outside the model in one of three ways:

  • Partial synchrony (Dwork, Lynch and Stockmeyer, 1988): delays have a bound that holds most of the time, but nobody knows when. Use timeouts to suspect crashed nodes, and accept that the suspicion is sometimes wrong. When the network behaves, the algorithm finishes; when it doesn't, it stalls but never disagrees. The Faults, time and truth track's lesson on system models introduced it; Paxos, Raft, Zab and Viewstamped Replication all live in it.
  • Failure detectors (Chandra and Toueg, 1996) package the timeouts as an oracle that may be wrong for a while but is eventually right about some correct node.
  • Randomness (Ben-Or, 1983): flip coins, and the chance of running forever shrinks to zero.

Paxos shows FLP from the algorithm's side. Two proposers can keep overtaking each other: P1 prepares 1.1, P2 prepares 2.2 before P1's accept arrives, P1 retries with 3.1 before P2's accept arrives, and so on. Lamport's fix is to pick one distinguished proposer, a leader, and to elect one you need either randomness or real time. The Try-it runs exactly this race and changes only the timing. Safety never moves; progress depends entirely on the timeout.

try.title: Make Paxos stall without breaking it
steps: Run PaxosDemo with -Pargs=timing. Two proposers, five acceptors, one-way delays of 1 to 30 ms (so a round trip can take 60 ms), and a proposer abandons a round after its timeout. Each line is 1,000 seeded runs, stopped after 2 seconds.
Before you run it, predict how many runs decide with a 20 ms timeout, and how many choose two values in any configuration.

20 ms      at once                        1 of 1,000          204.5             0
20 ms      random backoff                97 of 1,000          169.0             0
40 ms      at once                      477 of 1,000           93.3             0

With a 20 ms timeout, shorter than a round trip, proposers abandon rounds before the answers can arrive: 1 run of 1,000 decided when retrying at once, 97 with random backoff, each after hundreds of rounds. From 60 ms up every run decides, in a handful of rounds. The last column never moves: in all 8,000 runs no two values were chosen. Timing decides whether Paxos finishes, never what it decides. Raft's randomized election timeouts in the next lesson are the same fix.

sections.h: Paxos in plain words, and the family it started
sections.html:
Leslie Lamport's Paxos decides one value among acceptors (usually 3 or 5 nodes), on behalf of proposers that want different values chosen. Every attempt carries a ballot number that no other proposer uses: here (round, proposer id), so 2.2 beats 1.1. A value is chosen once a majority of acceptors have accepted it under the same ballot. Each acceptor stores two things on disk: the highest ballot it has promised, and the last proposal it accepted.

Phase 1, prepare and promise. A proposer picks a new ballot b and sends prepare(b) to the acceptors. An acceptor that hasn't promised anything higher promises b (it will never again accept a lower ballot) and replies with the last proposal it accepted, if any.

Phase 2, accept. With promises from a majority, the proposer chooses a value: the value of the highest-numbered accepted proposal among the replies, or its own value if none was reported. It sends accept(b, value). An acceptor accepts unless it has promised a higher ballot since.

The stepper plays a run where the first proposer crashes right after its value was chosen. Why does the second one end up with the same value? Any two majorities share at least one acceptor. If a value v was chosen under ballot b, a majority accepted it. A later proposer's phase 1 must hear from a majority, so it hears from at least one acceptor that accepted v. The highest-numbered rule makes it adopt v (or a later proposal that, by the same argument, already carries v). So once chosen, a value stays chosen. Messages can be lost, duplicated or reordered, and acceptors can crash and restart from disk, without breaking this. Forget the disk, and it breaks: the Try-it shows both.

Single-decree Paxos decides one value in two round trips. Real systems need a log, so they run Multi-Paxos: a stable leader runs phase 1 once, for all future log slots, and then each command needs only phase 2, one round trip. A new leader fills any gaps it finds with no-op entries. Chubby, Spanner and DynamoDB's partition replication all use Multi-Paxos.

Two relatives grew up separately. Viewstamped Replication (Oki and Liskov, 1988, revised by Liskov and Cowling in 2012) has a primary that orders requests and a view-change protocol to replace it, where a view number plays the ballot's role. Zab is ZooKeeper's atomic broadcast: an epoch number per leader, and every transaction id (zxid) is the epoch in its high 32 bits plus a counter. They share one skeleton: a number that increases with each leader, a majority to install the leader, a majority to commit each entry, and the guarantee that the two majorities overlap. Raft, the next lesson, is that skeleton written down so that you can implement it.

stepper.title: One Paxos decision, with a crash in the middle
stepper.intro: Ballots are written round.proposer, so 2.2 is round 2 from P2. Each acceptor's promise and accepted proposal are on its disk.

frames.say: A2 raises its promise to 2.2 and tells P2 what it accepted: ballot 1.1, capture. A3 promises too (P1's old prepare, if it ever arrives, is now below its promise). P2 has a majority of promises, and one of them carries a value.

frames.say: Here is the rule that makes Paxos safe. P2 must propose the value of the highest-numbered proposal among the promises, which is capture, and not its own void. It sends accept(2.2, capture), and both acceptors accept.

frames.say: P2 hears accepted(2.2) from a majority and learns the decision: capture, the same value that was chosen in frame 3. It had to be: any two majorities of three share an acceptor, here A2, and the phase-1 answers made P2 hear about the chosen value before it could propose anything else.

try.title: Break the rule, break the disk
steps: Run PaxosDemo. Three proposers (capture, void, refund), five acceptors, 20% of messages lost, 10% duplicated, up to two acceptors down at a time, and all but one proposer crash early. 500 seeded runs per line.

The second line replaces the highest-numbered rule with "always propose your own value". The third makes acceptors forget their promises and accepts when they restart, as if they acknowledged before writing to disk. Predict all three "two different values" counts first.
try.expect:
3 proposers (capture, void, refund), 5 acceptors, 20% of messages lost, 10% duplicated,
up to 2 acceptors down at a time, all but one proposer crash early

Paxos as written
  runs where someone learned a decision: 500 of 500
  runs where two different values were chosen: 0
  rounds per run: mean 7.8, max 43

proposers ignore the promises and push their own value
  runs where someone learned a decision: 500 of 500
  runs where two different values were chosen: 114
  rounds per run: mean 7.8, max 43

acceptors forget their promises when they restart
  runs where someone learned a decision: 500 of 500
  runs where two different values were chosen: 36
  rounds per run: mean 7.7, max 43

Written correctly, Paxos survived all of it: lost and duplicated messages, crashed acceptors and proposers, and no run chose two values. Drop the highest-numbered rule and 114 runs chose two values: a later proposer overwrote a value that was already chosen. Let acceptors forget and 36 runs split: an acceptor that promised 2.2 and lost the promise can accept an older ballot again, so two majorities stop sharing what they know. That is the NATS JetStream failure Jepsen found in 2025, where Raft nodes acknowledged writes they had only flushed to disk every two minutes.

refs.title: Ongaro and Ousterhout, In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (the Raft paper, PDF)

sections.html:
Consensus gives you a leader that can be replaced without losing or forking anything. Four costs come with it.

Start with majorities. Tolerating f crashed nodes takes 2f + 1: three nodes survive one failure, five survive two. A fourth node buys nothing, because a majority of four is three, so four still survive only one. Kafka's KRaft documentation gives the same rule for its controllers: run three or five. The side of a partition without a majority can't decide anything, which is CAP from lesson 1 again.

Then round trips and disks. Classic Paxos takes two round trips to a majority per value; Multi-Paxos and Raft take one per command once a leader is stable. Every acceptor must write its promise or its accepted entry to disk before answering, so each step costs an fsync too: often under a millisecond on an SSD, about 10 ms on a spinning disk. In the Try-it, a decision costs 4 messages per acceptor and about 22 ms with both phases, and half of each with phase 2 alone. Reads need care as well: a leader must confirm it is still the leader before it answers a linearizable read (lesson 4).

More nodes means fewer writes. Every write goes through the leader and needs a majority, so adding servers adds work to every write. The ZooKeeper paper (USENIX ATC 2010) measured a saturated ensemble:

ZooKeeper servers 3 5 7 9 13
writes per second, saturated 21,000 18,000 14,000 12,000 8,000
reads per second, saturated 87,000 165,000 257,000 296,000 460,000

Reads rise with the server count because ZooKeeper serves them from the local replica without consensus, which also makes them possibly stale. Writes fall. To get more write throughput you split the data into many independent consensus groups (shards), the way CockroachDB, TiKV and Spanner run one group per range of keys.

The fourth is timeouts. Too long, and a dead leader means a long outage. Too short, and slow round trips look like failures, as the timing Try-it showed. The next lesson shows how Raft and etcd choose them.

Clever variants have a history, too. EPaxos (Moraru, Andersen and Kaminsky, SOSP 2013) removes the leader: any replica can commit a command in one round trip if no conflicting command is in flight. In 2019 Pierre Sutra found a bug, in both its TLA+ specification and its Go implementation, that let replicas disagree and broke linearizability. A 2021 re-evaluation (Tollman, Park and Ousterhout, NSDI) confirmed the lower median latency across regions but measured tail latency more than four times worse than Multi-Paxos. A 2025 paper reported a further bug, in which recovery can deadlock. Twelve years of expert attention, and the corrections kept coming. Use a consensus implementation that many systems run and test (etcd's Raft library, ZooKeeper, KRaft), and treat any homemade failover that isn't one as unsafe until proven otherwise.

try.title: Count the messages per decision
steps: Run PaxosDemo with -Pargs=cost: one proposer, no loss, delays of 1 to 10 ms, with 3, 5 and 7 acceptors. It reports messages and milliseconds per decision, for the whole round and for phase 2 alone (what Multi-Paxos pays per command once a leader holds its promises).
Predict: do more acceptors make a decision slower?
try.expect:
one proposer, no loss, one-way delay 1 to 10 ms, 1,000 runs per line
acceptors         messages    phase 2 only      ms, whole round     ms, phase 2 only
3                     11.9               6                 22.2                 11.0
5                     19.9              10                 22.0                 11.0
7                     27.9              14                 22.0                 10.9

Messages grow with the number of acceptors (about 4 per acceptor; slightly under because the run stops as soon as the decision is learned), and phase 2 alone is half the messages and half the time. Latency barely moves with more acceptors here, because the simulation has no disks and no CPU limit and the leader waits only for the fastest majority. On real servers each extra acceptor is more network and fsync work for the leader on every write, which is the ZooKeeper table's falling write rate.

refs.title: Hunt et al., ZooKeeper: Wait-free coordination for Internet-scale systems (USENIX ATC 2010, PDF)
Tollman, Park and Ousterhout, EPaxos Revisited (NSDI 2021)
Sutra, On the correctness of Egalitarian Paxos

analogy: A board of five directors must approve exactly one bid for a company, and they can only send letters, which may be delayed or lost. Each bid carries a ticket number. A broker first writes to the directors: "will you ignore every ticket below mine, and which bid, if any, have you already signed?" Once three directors promise, the broker must put forward the highest-ticket bid any of them has signed, or its own bid if none has, and asks them to sign it. When three directors have signed the same ticket, the bid is accepted, even if the broker's car breaks down on the way home. Any later broker writes to at least three directors, so at least one of them has signed it and says so. The analogy breaks at the filing cabinet: a real acceptor that loses its records after a crash (or never wrote them down) can sign a lower ticket again, and the whole guarantee goes.
world: You already run consensus, mostly without seeing it. Kafka 4.x elects its controller and orders cluster metadata with KRaft, a Raft dialect, which is why you run 3 or 5 controllers. Kubernetes stores every object in etcd (Raft). A Cassandra INSERT ... IF NOT EXISTS for an idempotency key runs a Paxos round on that partition. DynamoDB replicates each partition with Multi-Paxos. Temporal's history service relies on a database to order each workflow's events, and that database's own leader and replication rules decide whether an acknowledged event can be lost. The design lesson for your own services: don't write failover logic of the form "if the primary looks dead, promote me". Take the decision from one of these systems (an etcd lease with a fencing token, a database's conditional write), so that two pods can never both believe they are the payment-batch leader.
mistake: Building leader election or a unique-ID allocator on a heartbeat and a timeout: "if I haven't heard from the leader for 10 seconds, I'm the leader now." It works in every test, because in tests the old leader really is dead. In production the old leader was paused by a garbage collection or a slow disk, comes back, and both nodes act as leader; or a network split puts one on each side. People write it because it looks like what consensus does, and the failing case needs an unlucky pause. The fix is to take leadership from a consensus system (an etcd or ZooKeeper lease, a row lock or advisory lock on the database primary, a Kafka consumer group's partition assignment) and to fence every write with the epoch or token it gives you, as in the Faults, time and truth track's lesson on leases.

compare.title: Two-phase commit and Paxos both vote twice. They are not the same.

a.label: Two-phase commit
a.title: Two-phase commit
a.html:
who asks:     the coordinator only
who must say yes:  every participant
outcome:      commit only if all voted yes
if the asker dies: participants wait in doubt
               (blocking; locks held)
what it solves: atomic commit, assuming the
               coordinator comes back

b.label: Paxos
b.title: Paxos
b.html:
who asks:     any proposer, with a higher ballot
who must say yes:  a majority of acceptors
outcome:      one value, which never changes
if the asker dies: another proposer finishes,
               adopting any accepted value
what it solves: consensus, with up to f of
               2f + 1 acceptors down

compare.note: Both have a prepare round and a commit round, so they get confused. The difference is who is allowed to finish. In two-phase commit only the coordinator can, and it needs every participant. In Paxos anyone can start a new ballot, a majority is enough, and the promise round makes sure the new proposer learns anything already chosen. Fault-tolerant atomic commit puts the two together: the vote rule from 2PC, with the decision made by consensus.

worked.title: Decide what to do with an in-doubt payment, safely

steps.say: The problem: a payment coordinator decides capture or void for pay-77, and it can crash. Write down the safety property first.
steps.code:
property: every service that learns the outcome of pay-77 learns the same outcome
threats:  coordinator crash, a second coordinator taking over, lost messages

steps.say: The tempting design: whoever finds the decision missing writes one. Two coordinators can both find it missing and write different outcomes. That is check-then-act, the race from the Transactions track.
steps.code: // unsafe: read, then write if (store.get("decision:pay-77") == null) { store.put("decision:pay-77", "capture") // another coordinator may write "void" here too }

steps.say: Replace it with consensus in its compare-and-set disguise: one atomic operation on a linearizable register, and use the value it reports, not your own.
steps.code: // safe: the first CAS wins, everyone adopts the winner val before = register.compareAndExchange("decision:pay-77", expected = null, value = "capture") val outcome = before ?: "capture" // someone decided first: use theirs

steps.say: Get that register from something that already runs consensus. With etcd, a transaction that creates the key only if it doesn't exist is that CAS (lesson 5 covers etcd).
steps.code:
etcdctl txn <<'EOF'
create("decision/pay-77") = "0"

put decision/pay-77 capture

get decision/pay-77

EOF

steps.say: Check liveness separately: if the etcd cluster loses its majority, the CAS can't complete. Decide what the coordinator does then (retry with backoff, alert), and never fall back to the unsafe read-then-write.
steps.code:
no majority -> CAS times out -> outcome unknown -> retry the SAME CAS later
(the CAS is idempotent: retrying returns the value that won)

lab.title: Paxos on a hostile network, and a register on a log
steps: Run the tests from the labs folder (no Docker, about a second). All 17 fail. Skim Sim.kt (virtual time; a network that loses, duplicates and reorders) and runPaxos at the bottom of Paxos.kt, which delivers messages, crashes nodes and restarts rounds. You write the rules, not the plumbing.
Exercise 1, Acceptor.onPrepare and onAccept: promise or accept unless you've promised a higher ballot (an equal one is fine, for duplicates); a promise carries what you last accepted.

Exercise 2, chooseValue and Proposer.onPromise: ignore other ballots, count each acceptor once, and at the first majority return the Accept with the value of the highest accepted ballot, or your own. Exercise 3, Proposer.onAccepted: at a majority, set decided.

PaxosTest checks each rule; PaxosPropertyTest runs 500 random hostile configurations and requires that no two values are ever chosen, plus a liveness test and a check that the test catches a broken value rule.

Exercises 4 to 6 in LogRegister.kt: Replica.apply (the state machine: return the value before, swap on a match), LogRegister.submit (remember the callback, broadcast), and propose (consensus from one compare-and-exchange). LogRegisterTest checks the seat race, identical replica logs and linearizability of 200 recorded histories.
hints: onPrepare: val p = promised; if (p != null && m.ballot < p) return Reject(m.ballot, p), then set promised and return Promise(m.ballot, acceptedBallot, acceptedValue).
In onPromise, return null once proposed is set, so a late promise doesn't send a second Accept with a different value.
propose is one line: register.compareAndExchange(client, null, value) { before -> done(before ?: value) }.

drill.title: The Paxos rules, from memory
drill.prompt: Write the acceptor's two handlers and the proposer's value rule for single-decree Paxos. State, in one comment each, which line would break safety if you dropped it.

answer.html: fun onPrepare(m: Prepare): Message { val p = promised if (p != null && m.ballot < p) return Reject(m.ballot, p) // without it: an old proposer's round could still finish promised = m.ballot // on disk before replying, or a restart forgets the promise return Promise(m.ballot, acceptedBallot, acceptedValue) // without the accepted value, a chosen value can be overwritten } fun onAccept(m: Accept): Message { val p = promised if (p != null && m.ballot < p) return Reject(m.ballot, p) // without it: accept a ballot you promised to ignore promised = m.ballot acceptedBallot = m.ballot acceptedValue = m.value return Accepted(m.ballot, m.value) } fun chooseValue(own: String, promises: Collection<Promise>): String = promises.filter { it.accepted != null }.maxByOrNull { it.accepted!! }?.value ?: own // the safety rule

recap: Total order broadcast delivers the same messages in the same order everywhere; with deterministic code on each replica (state machine replication) that keeps replicas identical. A fixed sequencer is the simplest version and fails with its sequencer.

Consensus (agreement, integrity, validity, termination), linearizable compare-and-set, total order broadcast and fault-tolerant atomic commit reduce to each other. Fetch-and-add is weaker: consensus number 2.

FLP: in an asynchronous model, no deterministic algorithm can guarantee termination with one crash. Real algorithms stay safe always and use timeouts (partial synchrony), failure detectors or randomness to make progress.

Paxos: prepare and promise, then accept with the value of the highest-numbered accepted proposal. Any two majorities overlap, so a chosen value stays chosen, provided acceptors keep their promises on disk.
Multi-Paxos runs phase 1 once and pays one round trip per command; Viewstamped Replication and Zab are the same skeleton of epoch, majority to elect, majority to commit. Raft is next.

The cost: 2f + 1 nodes for f failures, a round trip and an fsync per write, falling write throughput as nodes are added (ZooKeeper: 21,000 writes a second at 3 servers, 8,000 at 13), timeouts to tune, and subtle bugs in clever variants such as EPaxos.

explain.prompt: An architect proposes replacing etcd with "a simple heartbeat: the node with the lowest ID that's alive is the leader". Explain to them why that isn't enough, and what consensus gives that the heartbeat doesn't.
explain.answer: The heartbeat scheme decides who is leader from each node's own view of who is alive, and those views can differ. If node 1 is paused by a long garbage collection, node 2 stops hearing it and takes over; when node 1 wakes up, it still thinks it is leader, and for a while both accept writes. A network split does the same thing permanently: each side sees a different lowest live ID. Consensus avoids this because a node becomes leader only when a majority votes for it under a new, higher epoch number, and any two majorities share a node, so two leaders can't both be confirmed for the same epoch. Every write is committed only once a majority has it, so a new leader is guaranteed to have every committed write. The epoch also works as a fencing token, so the database can reject writes from an old leader that wakes up. What consensus can't promise is progress during a bad partition, but it never lets two nodes both be right about being leader, which is the property the payment batch needs.

deeper.html:
Lamport first described Paxos in "The Part-Time Parliament", written around 1990 as the story of a Greek island's legislature and published in ACM TOCS in 1998. Reviewers found the story hard to read, and "Paxos Made Simple" (2001) restated it in plain terms; it also describes Multi-Paxos and the gap-filling no-ops. "Paxos Made Live" (Chandra, Griesemer and Redstone, 2007) is Google's account of what it took to turn the algorithm into Chubby's replicated log: disk corruption, master leases, snapshots and group membership, none of which the paper covers.

Flexible Paxos (Howard, Malkhi and Spiegelman, 2016) showed that majorities are more than you need: only the phase-1 quorums must intersect the phase-2 quorums. With six acceptors you could, for example, use any four for leader election and any three for each command. Production systems mostly keep majorities, because they are simpler to reason about when membership changes.

Herlihy's 1991 paper on wait-free synchronization ranks shared objects by consensus number: read/write registers have 1, test-and-set, fetch-and-add, queues and stacks have 2, and compare-and-set has infinity. It is why java.util.concurrent is built on compareAndSet.

Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, chapter 10 presents the consensus equivalences and the common structure of Raft, Paxos, Zab and Viewstamped Replication.
